subjects.title: Optimisation
subjects.intro: Follow an optimization proof from its objective and access model to a quantitative guarantee. Browse mathematical foundations separately from formal libraries, AI tools and new papers.

route.title: Specify the problem
route.text: State the feasible set, geometry, convexity and smoothness assumptions. Fix the oracle and whether the guarantee is an objective gap, stationarity or feasibility.

route.title: Choose the mechanism
route.text: Start with a one-step descent or potential inequality. Distinguish gradient, proximal, mirror, accelerated and block methods rather than treating all convergence proofs as interchangeable.

route.title: Check the guarantee
route.text: Track constants, step sizes, initialization and the actual oracle count. Read lower bounds and counterexamples under the same access model.

subjects.boundary: External methods and theorem candidates are reference material. Existing local proofs and source coverage are reported only by their canonical publication pages.

subjects.title: Sampling
subjects.intro: Begin with the target, state space and access model. Choose a sampling regime before a named algorithm; use the textbook for foundations and SampleWiki for research results.

route.title: Specify the experiment
route.text: Record the target law, continuous or discrete state, initialization and permitted oracle. A sampler must define an actual measurable random output or probability kernel.

route.title: Separate the proof obligations
route.text: Construction, non-explosion, invariance, convergence and implementation bias are different results. Discrete sampling is not the numerical discretization of a continuous process.

route.title: Compose errors and costs
route.text: Match TV, Wasserstein, KL or another discrepancy to the theorem. Track conditional errors and costs under the actual input law; TV proximity alone does not control an unbounded expected query count.

subjects.boundary: Optimization primitives can support a sampling proof but cannot replace kernel semantics, integrability, domain assumptions, a mixing estimate or a cost theorem.

subjects.title: Geometry and transport
subjects.intro: Keep the ambient space, metric and geometric structure visible. Read manifold optimization and statistical transport together where useful, without identifying their different notions of gradient or curvature.

route.title: Choose the space
route.text: Specify manifold, tangent space, Riemannian metric, retraction or geodesic. For transport, state measures, moments, couplings and the transport cost.

route.title: Identify the adapter
route.text: Ask which Euclidean ingredient survives and which metric-dependent inequality must be proved anew. A similar proof diagram is not a theorem that transports between spaces.

route.title: Expose the boundary
route.text: Distinguish geodesic convexity, displacement convexity and analytic curvature assumptions. Check completeness, cut loci, optimizer existence and moment hypotheses where the argument uses them.

subjects.boundary: Title-based discovery links below suggest reading, not source equivalence or a certified Euclidean-to-Riemannian/Wasserstein transport.

Differential.title: Differential calculus
Differential.purpose: Gradients, chain/product rules, mean-value and Taylor arguments.
Differential.consumer: Shared analytic floor for Euclidean energy estimates. Riemannian gradients require their own tangent-space and metric adapter.

Convex.title: Convex analysis
Convex.purpose: Convexity, strong convexity, subgradients, cones and separation.
Convex.consumer: Potential curvature can feed log-concavity prerequisites. It does not by itself prove a functional inequality, mixing bound or invariant law.

Function.title: Smoothness and proximal structure
Function.purpose: Smoothness models, lower semicontinuity, proximal maps and Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz structure.
Function.consumer: A proximal minimizer and a Gibbs/RGO draw are different objects. Also distinguish Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz properties from Kullback–Leibler divergence.

Optimality.title: Optimality and duality
Optimality.purpose: Unconstrained stationarity, constraint qualifications, KKT and weak duality.
Optimality.consumer: Transport and constrained algorithms need their own primal/dual spaces, attainment and constraint qualifications; do not infer them from an analogy.

Algorithm.title: Algorithms and complexity
Algorithm.purpose: Gradient/subgradient methods, proximal gradient, acceleration, LASSO, BCD and ADMM.
Algorithm.consumer: Compare actual updates, potential estimates and oracle models. No optimization convergence theorem is silently promoted into sampling complexity.
